title: What Gives a Worthless Thing Value? The Puzzle of Money
question: A dollar bill is just paper, and most money today is not even paper. Why does everyone agree it's worth something?
summary: Money has no intrinsic use, yet it commands universal acceptance. Understanding why reveals money as one of humanity's strangest and most powerful collective fictions.
content:
Pick up a banknote and look at it honestly: it's a small rectangle of cotton-linen fiber with ink on it, worth perhaps a fraction of a cent as raw material. Most money isn't even that—it's a number in a bank's database, adjusted by electrical signals. And yet people will work exhausting jobs, forgo sleep, and organize entire lives around acquiring more of it. Unlike food, shelter, or tools, money has essentially no use value of its own. You cannot eat it, and holding a pile of cash and warmth does nothing for your body. So what, exactly, makes something worth something?

Money as a Solved Coordination Problem

The classic economic story starts with barter's inconvenience. If you have wheat and want shoes, you need a shoemaker who happens to want wheat—a "double coincidence of wants" that's often rare. Money solves this by acting as a universally acceptable intermediate good: you sell your wheat for money to anyone, then use that money to buy shoes from anyone. Its value isn't in what it is, but in what almost everyone else will accept it for. This makes money less like an object and more like a widely shared agreement, a coordination device that lets a society of self-interested strangers exchange value without needing to trust one another's specific desires, only trust the token itself.

The Fiction That Works Only If Everyone Believes It

This is where money starts to look less like an ordinary economic tool and more like a shared hallucination that happens to be extraordinarily useful. A dollar has value because you believe the next person will accept it, and they believe the same about the person after that, in a chain of trust that ultimately terminates nowhere in particular—no gold vault, no promise redeemable for a fixed quantity of anything physical, since most modern currencies left the gold standard behind decades ago. Anthropologists point out that this isn't a flaw unique to modern fiat currency; even historical "commodity money" like cowrie shells, salt, or gold coins derived much of their power from social agreement and ritual significance as much as practical utility. Gold is shiny and rare, but rarity alone doesn't explain why humans across unconnected civilizations converged on similar objects as stores of value.

Trust as Infrastructure

What actually backs a modern currency is not metal but institutions: a government's capacity to tax, a central bank's credibility, courts that enforce contracts, and a population's collective habit of using the currency daily. This is why hyperinflation is so psychologically devastating—it's not just that prices rise, it's that the shared fiction starts visibly cracking, and the moment enough people start doubting the story, the value can collapse far faster than any physical scarcity would predict. Confidence isn't a side effect of monetary value; it is the substance of monetary value.

Money as Technology, Not Substance

Seen this way, money resembles language more than it resembles gold. A word has no innate connection to its meaning—"dog" doesn't look or sound like a dog—but it works because a whole community has converged on the same convention, and that convention lets minds coordinate with astonishing efficiency. Money is a similarly arbitrary symbol system, except the thing it lets people coordinate isn't meaning but claims on future goods and labor. Cryptocurrencies pushed this insight to its logical extreme: a currency with no government, no physical form, and no institutional backing at all, whose entire value rests on a decentralized network's shared belief that the ledger will keep being honored. That such a system can acquire real value at all is either the ultimate proof that money was always a social fiction, or a cautionary tale about how thin that fiction can become.

perspectives.title: Economic Perspective
perspectives.description: Money functions as a medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value, solving the double coincidence of wants that makes pure barter economies inefficient at scale.

perspectives.title: Anthropological Perspective
perspectives.description: Historical commodity monies (shells, salt, cattle, gold) derived value from social and ritual significance as much as scarcity, suggesting money predates and exceeds pure market logic.

perspectives.title: Political Perspective
perspectives.description: Modern fiat currency's value rests on state power: the ability to tax in that currency, enforce contracts, and maintain institutional credibility, which is why currency collapse tracks state collapse.

perspectives.title: Philosophical Perspective
perspectives.description: Money is best understood as a collectively maintained social fact, a fiction that becomes real precisely because enough people act as though it is, similar to the way laws, borders, or corporations exist.

perspectives.title: Technological Perspective
perspectives.description: Cryptocurrency experiments strip away governments and physical tokens entirely, testing how much shared belief alone, encoded in a protocol, can substitute for institutional backing.

connections: Social constructs and collective belief (John Searle's 'social facts')
The gold standard and its abandonment
Hyperinflation and currency collapse (Weimar Germany, Zimbabwe)
The history of the barter myth in economic anthropology
Language as a system of arbitrary but shared conventions
openQuestions: If money's value depends entirely on collective belief, what other seemingly solid parts of society are actually the same kind of fiction?
Could a currency ever be designed that doesn't require any centralized trust anchor, and would people actually adopt it at scale?
Why do some fictions (national currencies) prove remarkably durable across centuries while others (failed currencies) collapse in months?
Does the increasing abstraction of money, from coins to paper to digital numbers, change what money fundamentally is, or only its form?
